writingRules: Cite ONLY figures present in this sheet. Do not introduce any new statistic from memory.
Every workforce/degree share MUST state its denominator (broad STEM vs core science & engineering vs by-field). Never present women's STEM share as a single bare number.

Present the Scully Effect, Freeman active-learning, Heckman ROI, and Tutor CoPilot strictly as SUGGESTIVE/analogous evidence drawn from OTHER populations (adults recalling 1990s TV; undergraduates; human tutors; intensive birth-to-five programs) — NOT as proof that PARI's ages-3-8 story+kit+AI model yields these outcomes. Always name the population.
Date-flag every survey stat (year + sponsor). The Junior Achievement 2019 teen figure is DROPPED; use ROX Girls' Index (2024) for girls' confidence/interest decline.
For market sizing use ONLY the reconciled figures in market_size; do not cite discarded outliers (GVR Horizon $13.66B; Global Market Insights $1.8B STEM-toys).
Any claim about PARI's OWN efficacy, retention, churn, or unit economics must be labeled a hypothesis / illustrative projection to be validated — never an established result.
Evidence-first tone; acknowledge limitations candidly. The goal is to survive adversarial diligence, not to oversell.
reconciliationNotes: US educational toys market: canonical = $12.19B (2023) growing 10.8% CAGR to ~$24.9B by 2030 (Grand View Research); corroborated by Custom Market Insights (~$24.6B by 2033, 9.2% CAGR). DROPPED the GVR 'Horizon' $13.66B-by-2030 figure as a narrower-scope outlier inconsistent with the same firm's CAGR.

US STEM-toys segment: reported as a wide range by definition. Conservative/reputable = US ~$340M (2024), the ~80% US share of GVR's North America STEM-toys market of $425.9M (2024 -> $629.2M by 2030, 6.6% CAGR). A broader vendor (Global Market Insights) puts US STEM-toys ~$1.8B (2024). Use educational toys ($12B) as the primary category TAM and cite STEM-toys as a fast-growing slice with the range disclosed.

Women's STEM-workforce share: standardized on NCSES/NSF (2023): ~35% of the broad 36M-person STEM workforce, but only ~27% of core science & engineering occupations, ~16% of engineers, ~26% of computer/mathematical scientists; ~24% of engineering and ~22% of computing bachelor's degrees (2021). Dropped standalone 24%/26%/2019-Census figures to avoid an unexplained 24-35% swing.
STEM job growth: canonical = +10.4% (2023-2033, BLS) vs +3.6% non-STEM. Dropped older +7% (2022-2032).

PISA 2022: US math 465 = below OECD average (28th of 37 OECD; 25 of 80 systems higher); US science 499 vs 485 OECD average (only 9 of 80 systems higher). Present both honestly; the weakness is in math.
Screen time (Common Sense 2025) is age-banded: under 2 = 1h03m/day; 2-4 = 2h08m; 5-8 = 3h28m; ~2.5h is the 0-8 average. Gaming time up 65% over four years.

education_state.claim: Only 31% of US 8th graders reached NAEP Proficient in science in 2024 (down 4 pts from 2019); 38% scored below NAEP Basic, the highest share since 2009
In 2024 only 22% of US 12th graders were proficient in math (45% below Basic, a record) and 35% proficient in reading (a record low)
From 2019 to 2024 average NAEP math scores fell 3 pts (4th grade) and 8 pts (8th grade); reading fell 5 pts at each grade
On PISA 2022 US 15-year-olds scored 465 in math (below the OECD average; 28th of 37 OECD members; 25 of 80 systems higher); science was 499 vs the 485 OECD average (only 9 systems higher)
education_state.src: NCES / OECD PISA; Pew Research for OECD rank

education_state.claim: US K-3 classrooms average just 18 minutes/day on science vs 89 on reading/language arts and 57 on math; grades 4-6 average 27 minutes on science
Science is taught every school day in only 17% of K-3 classes and 35% of grades 4-6 classes, versus nearly all classes for math
Only 31% of self-contained US elementary teachers feel 'very well prepared' to teach science (vs 77% reading, 73% math); only ~3% hold a science degree
US STEM occupations are projected to grow 10.4% from 2023 to 2033, nearly triple the 3.6% projected for non-STEM occupations
US STEM occupations had a median wage of $101,650 (May 2023), more than double the $46,680 non-STEM median
There were 36 million STEM workers in the US in 2023, about 24% of the total workforce

early_childhood.claim: By age 6, US girls become less likely than boys to associate brilliance ('really, really smart') with their own gender and begin avoiding activities described as for the 'really, really smart' — a gap absent at age 5

Racial/ethnic gaps in advanced (top-decile) science and math achievement are already present at kindergarten entry (~13-16% of White students vs 3-4% of Black or Hispanic students) and persist or widen through 5th grade
Across six US longitudinal datasets, kindergarten-entry math skills were the single strongest predictor of later achievement in both math and reading — ahead of early reading and attention
The share of US 8th-graders reporting high interest and enjoyment in science fell from 38% (2019) to 28% (2024), with a parallel decline in hands-on inquiry participation
75% of US Gen Z (12-26) report interest in STEM, but only 29% list a STEM role as their first-choice career
Among US Gen Z, 63% of girls express interest in STEM vs 85% of boys — a 22-point gender gap

A high-quality birth-to-five program for disadvantaged US children (ABC/CARE) delivered ~13% annual ROI (benefit-cost 6.3) — evidence for the VALUE OF EARLY-CHILDHOOD TIMING, not a consumer-product return
early_childhood.src: Heckman et al., University of Chicago

gender_gap.claim: Of the 36 million US STEM workers in 2023, ~35% were women (65% men); women are only ~27% of core science & engineering occupations despite being ~48% of the overall workforce
Women are ~16% of US engineers and ~26% of computer and mathematical scientists (2021)
In 2021 women earned ~24% of engineering and ~22% of computing bachelor's degrees, though they earned roughly half of all science & engineering bachelor's degrees

In a meta-analysis of 78 US Draw-A-Scientist studies (20,000+ children), the share drawing a female scientist rose from <1% (1966-77) to 28% (1985-2016), but the tendency to draw a male scientist still strengthens with age: ~70% of 6-year-old girls draw a woman scientist vs only ~25% of 16-year-old girls
gender_gap.src: Miller, Nolla, Eagly & Uttal, Child Development

gender_gap.claim: The share of US girls who believe they are good at math and science fell from 73% (2017) to 59% (2024); 58% of girls in grades 9-12 say they don't believe they are smart enough for their dream job (up from 46% in 2017); among 5th-6th graders it jumped from 23% to 52%

A single guest lecture by a woman economist raised women undergraduates' likelihood of majoring in economics by 8 points (9%->17%); same-gender STEM role models raised high-performing women's choice of underrepresented STEM majors by up to 26 points — ROLE-MODEL EVIDENCE FROM UNDERGRADUATES, suggestive for younger ages

Across 15 years of top US TV/film (2007-2022), women were ~38% of STEM characters (2018-22); female engineers just 13% and computer scientists 15% of those roles; 71% of surveyed respondents said female STEM representation on-screen is important (up 20 pts since 2018)
gender_gap.src: Geena Davis Institute (with IF/THEN, Lyda Hill Philanthropies)

screen_time.claim: US screen media per day by age (2025): under 2 = 1h03m; ages 2-4 = 2h08m; ages 5-8 = 3h28m; the 0-8 average is ~2.5 hours
40% of US children have their own tablet by age 2 and nearly 1 in 4 have a personal cellphone by age 8; gaming time among kids 8 and under surged 65% over four years
The AAP discourages screen media (besides video chat) under 18 months and recommends limiting ages 2-5 to ~1 hour/day of high-quality programming, reserving time for free play

The US Surgeon General's 2023 advisory warns that up to 95% of youth 13-17 use social media (a third 'almost constantly') and ~40% of children 8-12 do; >3 hours/day of social media is associated with roughly double the risk of poor mental-health outcomes
42% of US parents of children 12 and under say they could do better managing their child's screen time, and 80% say social media does more harm than good for kids

parent_demand.claim: 94% of US parents say toys play a significant role in their child's development and 91% emphasize the importance of educational toys; 78% want more toys that build skills like creativity and problem-solving, with screen-free, maker-style kits flagged as leading purchase trends
76% of US parents say they want their child to end up in a STEM-related career (survey of 2,000 parents) — vendor/advocacy survey, treat as directional
Only 28% of US adults rate US K-12 STEM education as 'best in the world or above average'; 32% call it below average or worst

89% of US parents believe their child is at or above grade level; once they learn a child is behind, worry spikes (97% of parents who know their child is below grade level in math are worried) — an awareness gap

High-income US families spend ~$8,900 per child per year on enrichment vs ~$1,300 for the lowest-income quintile — a gap that widened from ~4x to ~7x; an equity problem premium products must address, not worsen
US back-to-school spending reached a record ~$890 per family with K-12 children (2023 NRF) and a projected ~$886/household in 2025

In a US hands-on educational-subscription category, Lovevery's 24-month lifetime sales per customer reached $692.38 — more than double KiwiCo's and Little Passports' — signaling strong willingness to pay for premium hands-on learning

market_size.claim: US educational toys market ~$12.19B (2023), growing 10.8% CAGR to ~$24.9B by 2030; corroborated by an independent estimate of ~$24.6B by 2033 (9.2% CAGR). STEM/hands-on learning is the fastest-growing driver within the category
market_size.src: Grand View Research; Custom Market Insights
market_size.verify: Confirm GVR base-year value, CAGR, and 2030 endpoint; confirm the discarded $13.66B Horizon figure is a narrower scope.

market_size.claim: North America STEM-toys market $425.9M (2024) -> $629.2M by 2030 (6.6% CAGR); US ~80% share implies ~$340M (2024). A broader vendor definition puts US STEM-toys ~$1.8B (2024) — range disclosed
market_size.src: Grand View Research; Global Market Insights
market_size.verify: Confirm NA figure and US share.

market_size.claim: US EdTech market $47.74B (2024) -> $90.61B by 2030 (11.1% CAGR); K-12 was largest in 2024 and PRESCHOOL is the fastest-growing sector through 2030
US AI-in-education market projected to reach ~$8.84B by 2030 at a 31.2% CAGR (2025-2030) — the steepest growth among US education segments
US online private tutoring ~$4.33B (2024) -> ~$8.09B by 2030 (11.1% CAGR); total US private tutoring ~$39.6B (2024)
market_size.src: Grand View Research; Global Industry Analysts

competitors_base.claim: KiwiCo core monthly STEM crates $23.95/mo (premium Maker/Eureka $32.95/mo) — kit-only, no integrated app or serialized story
Lovevery Play Kits ~$40/mo effective (baby $80/2mo; toddler $120/3mo) — Montessori toy subscription, no app or narrative
MEL Science science-kit subscription $34.90/mo ($25.90/mo annual); Khan Academy Kids is 100% free (app-only); Osmo Genius Starter Kit ~$90 one-time (tablet-tethered)
More than one-third of US subscription consumers cancel within three months and ~40% ultimately cancel; for curation/access boxes 29% cite 'not getting value for the money' as the top reason
Subscription-box businesses typically face 10-15% monthly churn, among the highest-churn e-commerce categories — illustrative industry benchmark

efficacy_proxy.claim: Active (hands-on) learning raised undergraduate STEM exam performance by 0.47 SD, and lecture-only students were ~1.5x more likely to fail — UNDERGRADUATE evidence, suggestive (not established) for ages 3-8

Among US adult women, heavy female viewers of The X-Files were 50% more likely to have worked in STEM (24% vs 16%) and 63% named Dana Scully a personal role model — CORRELATIONAL, adults recalling a 1990s drama; suggestive only

In an RCT, US students of tutors using AI assistance (Tutor CoPilot) were 4 points more likely to master math topics (9 points for the lowest-rated tutors) — AI AUGMENTING HUMAN tutors, not a child-facing AI; suggestive
25% of US K-12 teachers say AI tools do more harm than good in education (only 6% more good); parents and educators flag trust and child-data concerns — a barrier PARI must design around

72% of US teens have used an AI companion and 52% are regular users; 1 in 3 find AI conversations as satisfying as those with real friends — context on AI adoption AND the need for guardrails for young children
